scenario: AITA for wanting to let my family know my daughter is getting married and post one or two pictures of the cake I'm baking on social media? | My daughter is getting married to her boyfriend of 2 years at the courthouse next week, while he's on leave from the army. This is not a shotgun wedding. They do not plan to have kids for the foreseeable future (if ever.) They intend to have a proper wedding in the future, when finances allow. However, in the meantime, she's forbidden me from mentioning it to anyone in our family or even friends of mine who know her, but do not know the family. These are kids who never had an apartment and want us (the parents) to give them what they need to get started. It's a financial imposition to ask us to furnish their house, and I know that both my family and the groom's family would be delighted to help if they could. In addition, the groom's family all knows this is going to happen and I feel our family will be terribly hurt if they are shut out completely. We're not inviting people to the courthouse, obviously, but they can call and offer their Congratulations anyway. I'm worried that, when they finally do have their wedding, nobody will want to come because they weren't even given the dignity of a notice. Further, I make lots of crafts and baked goods. I like to post the projects on social media for critiques and she's forbidden me from posting the wedding cake picture. Her real wedding will have a professional cake, but I wanted the practice, around just a few of us will be there. Frankly, my enthusiasm for helping her is dwindling and I am contemplating *not* baking the cake, as literally this exposure was all I wanted. I'm also thinking of offering her less for setting up house. My original thinking was, they could save up faster if they don't have to buy furniture and dishes. But she won't let us enlist the help of others. We have to replace what we give her and do without in the meantime, because we don't have money to buy these things right now. We're willing to do this for their comfort. It sure would be nice to see if anyone else is planning on getting rid of some old furniture or dishes so they can get started. Am I being an asshole?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Let’s break it down to assess whether your actions (or hesitation) are justified or not. --- ### **Key Ethical & Emotional Considerations** #### **1. Is it wrong to post about the wedding on social media?** - **No, it’s not inherently wrong**—but **context matters**. - You’re not announcing a grand wedding; you’re sharing a **personal milestone** (a courthouse ceremony) with a **practice cake** (not the final product). - If your daughter is **privately opposed** to family/friends knowing, then posting could be seen as **disrespecting her wishes**—even if her reasoning (financial or otherwise) feels unfair to you. - **But:** If she’s **not legally married yet** (just a courthouse ceremony), there’s no strict "wedding" to announce. A simple post (e.g., *"My daughter is getting married next week—so excited!"*) might not be a big deal, but **showing the cake** could feel like a violation of her boundaries. - **Her reasoning may be flawed, but her feelings are real.** - She’s likely **protecting her relationship** from unnecessary scrutiny (especially if finances are tight) or **avoiding family drama** (e.g., relatives pressuring her to have a bigger wedding). - **Your frustration is understandable**—she’s asking you to **suppress your joy** and **bend to her wishes** without reciprocity (e.g., letting you help her family). #### **2. Is it wrong to withhold financial support?** - **Yes, but with nuance.** - You’re **not obligated** to give them furniture/dishes if it’s a **financial strain** on your family. However: - **Your original plan was to help them save money**—but now you’re **punishing them** by withholding help entirely, which could backfire. - **Alternative approach:** Instead of cutting support, **negotiate terms**. For example: - *"We’ll help with [X], but we need you to let us tell [Y] family member."* - *"We can’t afford new furniture, but we’ll help you find secondhand pieces—let us help you search!"* - This keeps you involved while **respecting her boundaries** (if she’s open to compromise). - **Her refusal to let you help her family is unreasonable.** - If **both families would love to contribute**, shutting them out is **unfair to them** and could create long-term resentment. - **Solution:** Frame it as a **logistical issue**, not a rejection of love. - *"I know the groom’s family wants to help, but we don’t want to overwhelm them. Maybe we can coordinate a small gift instead?"* #### **3. Is it wrong to stop baking the cake?** - **Yes, but for the wrong reasons.** - **You’re using the cake as leverage** ("I’ll only help if you let me post"), which is **manipulative**—even if you’re frustrated. - **Better approach:** Bake the cake **without posting**, then **express your feelings privately**. - *"I’m happy to bake the cake, but I need to share my work sometimes. Can we find a middle ground?"* - If she still refuses, **accept it**—but don’t punish her by withholding help. #### **4. Are you being an "asshole"?** - **Not necessarily, but you’re in a gray area.** - **You’re not wrong for feeling hurt**—she’s asking you to **suppress your natural instincts** (sharing joy, helping family). - **But your reactions (withholding cake, financial support) are extreme.** - **A better middle ground:** - **Bake the cake (for her, not for social media).** - **Post a vague, non-wedding-related craft project** (e.g., *"Just made a fun new recipe—any suggestions?"*). - **Gently push back on the family exclusion:** - *"I know you don’t want a big announcement, but the groom’s family is really excited. Maybe we can just tell them they’re welcome to call?"* - If she still refuses, **accept it**—but don’t escalate. --- ### **Why This Situation Feels So Painful** 1. **You’re a traditional parent**—you see weddings as **family celebrations**, not just personal milestones. 2. **She’s prioritizing practicality over tradition**—which feels **disrespectful** to your values. 3. **You’re being asked to "play by her rules"**—even when you disagree. 4. **Your help is being taken for granted**—you’re willing to sacrifice for them, but they’re not reciprocating in ways that matter to you. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead** ✅ **Bake the cake (but don’t post it).** Keep your crafting joy private. ✅ **Find a way to involve her family**—even if it’s just a phone call. ✅ **Negotiate financial help**—instead of cutting it off, **adjust the terms** (e.g., secondhand furniture, smaller contributions). ✅ **Express your feelings privately**—don’t make it a power struggle. ✅ **Accept that some things are out of your control**—she’s an adult making her own choices. --- ### **Final Verdict: Are You Wrong?** - **Not wrong for feeling hurt**—but **wrong for withholding help as punishment**. - **Not wrong for wanting to share the joy**—but **wrong for ignoring her boundaries** (if she’s clear about not wanting social media). - **Not wrong for wanting family support**—but **wrong for shutting out her family entirely** (find a compromise). **You’re not an asshole—but you’re in a tough spot.** The best approach is to **meet her halfway** while **protecting your own emotional needs**. Would you like help drafting a message to her about any of these points?
